% Next lines make "int" acceptable in the optional arg to function but
% it doesn't do much yet. How should internal functions be marked?
% For now I simply marked the commands in red as in (don't use or rely
% on).

\keys_define:nn { l3doc/function }
  {
    int .value_forbidden:n = true ,
    int .code:n =
      {
        \bool_set_true:N \l__codedoc_macro_internal_bool
      } ,
    readonly .value_forbidden:n = true ,
    readonly .code:n =
      {
        \bool_set_true:N \l__interfacetwo_readonly_bool
      } ,
    user .value_forbidden:n = true ,
    user .code:n =
      {
        \bool_set_true:N \l__codedoc_macro_user_bool
      } ,
  }

\bool_new:N \l__codedoc_macro_user_bool

% Constants: data that is set up by the kernel (possibly in several
% steps, e.g., code added to a kernel hook during the format build)
% but must not be changed outside the kernel. Typeset like variables.
% Constants and read-only variables show "(constant)", "(constants)"
% or "(read-only)" instead of a syntax example.
\bool_new:N \l__interfacetwo_readonly_bool
\seq_new:N \l__interfacetwo_names_seq
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_marker:n #1
  {
    \begin{syntax}
      \normalfont \emph { (#1) }
    \end{syntax}
  }
\DeclareDocumentEnvironment { constant } { O{} +v }
  {
    \__codedoc_function:nnw {#1} {#2}
    \seq_set_split:Nnn \l__interfacetwo_names_seq { , } {#2}
    \seq_remove_all:Nn \l__interfacetwo_names_seq { }
    \__interfacetwo_marker:n
      {
        constant
        \int_compare:nNnT { \seq_count:N \l__interfacetwo_names_seq } > 1 { s }
      }
  }
  { \__codedoc_function_end: }
% Variables: the option "readonly" marks state that only the kernel
% should change.
\DeclareDocumentEnvironment { variable } { O{} +v }
  {
    \bool_set_false:N \l__interfacetwo_readonly_bool
    \__codedoc_function:nnw {#1} {#2}
    \bool_if:NT \l__interfacetwo_readonly_bool
      { \__interfacetwo_marker:n { read-only } }
  }
  { \__codedoc_function_end: }

\cs_set_protected:Npn \__codedoc_typeset_functions:
  {
    \small\ttfamily
    \__codedoc_target:
    \Hy@MakeCurrentHref { HD. \int_use:N \c@HD@hypercount }
    \__codedoc_date_compare:VNVF \l__codedoc_date_added_tl > \l__codedoc_base_date_tl
      { \tl_clear:N \l__codedoc_date_added_tl }
    \__codedoc_date_compare:VNVF \l__codedoc_date_updated_tl > \l__codedoc_base_date_tl
      { \tl_clear:N \l__codedoc_date_updated_tl }
    \group_begin:
      \bool_if:NT \l__codedoc_macro_internal_bool { \color{red}  }
      \bool_if:NT \l__codedoc_macro_user_bool     { \color{blue} }
      \begin{tabular} [t] { @{} l @{} >{\hspace{\tabcolsep}} r @{} }
        \toprule
        \__codedoc_function_extra_labels:
        \__codedoc_names_typeset:
        \__codedoc_typeset_dates:
        \bottomrule
      \end{tabular}
    \group_end:
    \normalfont\normalsize
  }

% Arrow for "expands to/results in" in examples. A text glyph (TU
% U+2192, TS1 fallback) rather than math, so it also works inside alltt
% and doesn't produce a math structure when tagging.
\NewDocumentCommand \textyields {} { \textrightarrow }

% Usage of commands outside the core (sweep over TeX Live
% texmf-dist/tex/latex). These lines are generated by
% interface2-usage/update-usage.py -- don't edit them by hand; put
% corrections into interface2-usage/config.toml and rerun the script.
% They are placed directly after \end{function} or
% \end{variable} (not inside) so that long lists can break across
% pages. The optional argument names the command (without backslash)
% when an entry documents several commands.
%
%  \modifiers     packages that redefine or patch a command (or set a
%                 constant); always printed in full as this shouldn't
%                 happen
%  \setters       packages that set a variable meant to be set (e.g.,
%                 \@currentlabel or \topsep)
%  \readers       packages that only use an internal ("int") command
%  \publicreaders packages that use a command that is fine to use;
%                 separate so that these lists can easily be dropped
%
% The source always records the complete list; \setters, \readers and
% \publicreaders print at most \UsageListMax names followed by the
% total. An empty list (command checked, no usage found) prints
% nothing.

\int_new:N \l__interfacetwo_max_int
\int_new:N \l__interfacetwo_count_int
\clist_new:N \l__interfacetwo_clist
\NewDocumentCommand \UsageListMax { m }
  { \int_set:Nn \l__interfacetwo_max_int {#1} }
\UsageListMax { 20 }

% The packages in "Modified by" lists are shown in red; to turn that
% off use \RenewDocumentCommand \ModifiersFormat {} {}
\NewDocumentCommand \ModifiersFormat {} { \color{red} }

\NewDocumentCommand \modifiers { o m }
  {
    \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn { Modified } { modified } {#1} {#2}
      \c_false_bool { \ModifiersFormat }
  }
\NewDocumentCommand \setters { o m }
  { \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn { Set } { set } {#1} {#2} \c_true_bool { } }
\NewDocumentCommand \readers { o m }
  { \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn { Used } { used } {#1} {#2} \c_true_bool { } }
\NewDocumentCommand \publicreaders { o m }
  { \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn { Used } { used } {#1} {#2} \c_true_bool { } }

% #6: formatting applied to the package list only
\cs_new_protected:Npn \__interfacetwo_usage:nnnnNn #1#2#3#4#5#6
  {
    \clist_set:Nn \l__interfacetwo_clist {#4}
    \clist_if_empty:NF \l__interfacetwo_clist
      {
        \par \addvspace { \smallskipamount }
        { \footnotesize \raggedright \noindent
          \textbf
            {
              \tl_if_novalue:nTF {#3}
                { #1 \c_space_tl by: }
                { \cs[no-index]{#3} \c_space_tl #2 \c_space_tl by: }
            } ~
          #6
          \bool_lazy_and:nnTF {#5}
            {
              \int_compare_p:nNn
                { \clist_count:N \l__interfacetwo_clist } > \l__interfacetwo_max_int
            }
            {
              \int_zero:N \l__interfacetwo_count_int
              \clist_map_inline:Nn \l__interfacetwo_clist
                {
                  \int_incr:N \l__interfacetwo_count_int
                  \int_compare:nNnTF \l__interfacetwo_count_int > \l__interfacetwo_max_int
                    { \clist_map_break: }
                    { \int_compare:nNnF \l__interfacetwo_count_int = 1 { , ~ } ##1 }
                }
              \c_space_tl \ldots \c_space_tl (total~of~ \clist_count:N \l__interfacetwo_clist
                \c_space_tl packages)
            }
            { \clist_use:Nn \l__interfacetwo_clist { , ~ } }
          \par
        }
      }
  }

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
  I spent a bit this afternoon on making a list of all \LaTeXe{}
  commands in the kernel as input for something like the
  \texttt{cmdguide} or as a reference manual named
  \texttt{interface2}.

  So far this only covers commands from \texttt{latex.ltx}. Those from
  related files would need adding too.

  In its present form it is not yet useful, but once more commands are
  sorted and documented \ldots\ Frank
\end{abstract}


\tableofcontents

\newpage


\section{Conventions}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \foo, \foovariant
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{foo} \oarg{optional arg} \Arg{mandatory arg}
  \end{syntax}
  General form of documentation for commands. Commands that share a
  common behavior/interface may be documented together like this.

  The syntax box gives one example with arguments. Commands that are
  not user-level and take no arguments (variables, constants,
  internal helpers) have no syntax box.
  Data that may change is documented as a variable; a variable that
  only the kernel should change is marked \emph{(read-only)}. Data
  that is set up by the kernel (possibly in several steps) and never
  changes afterwards is documented as a constant. A command that is not yet
  documented has no explanation afterwards.

  After an entry, lists of packages in \TeX\,Live give the usage of
  its commands outside the core: \enquote{Modified by} lists packages
  that redefine or patch a command, which normally shouldn't happen
  (always shown in full); \enquote{Set by} lists packages that set a
  variable that is meant to be set (such as \cs{@currentlabel} or
  \cs{topsep}); \enquote{Used by} lists packages that only use a
  command (not given for user commands). Long \enquote{Set by} and
  \enquote{Used by} lists show only the first names and the total.
  The lists come from an automated search of \texttt{tex/latex} that
  excludes the core bundles, so they are indicative only.

\end{function}
\modifiers[foovariant]{}
\publicreaders[foovariant]{}

\begin{function}[TF]
  {
    \foo
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fooF} \Arg{text arg} \Arg{false branch}
  \end{syntax}
  Conditionals using the \texttt{TF} convention are documented like
  this.  In \LaTeXe{} commands normally do not indicate the arguments
  they take (\texttt{TF} is one of the exceptions). But any other
  arguments aren't indicated so one has to \enquote{know}.

  In contrast,
  commands from the L3 programming layer always denote their argument
  signature in the name (via the \texttt{:} convention).
  
\end{function}

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \foo
  }
  Internal commands that should not be relied on are marked in red.
  
\end{function}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \foo
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{foo} 
  \end{syntax}
  %
  Document-level (user) commands are shown in blue. In addition
  commands that are mainly for class and package writer but can also
  be useful in the document preamble or inside the document are also
  marked this way. This means that basically all core commands
  documented in \emph{The LaTeX{} Companion}\cite{tlc3} are shown in
  blue.
  
\end{function}

\begin{function}[EXP]
  {
    \foo
  }
  Fully expandable functions, i.e., those that can be used
  inside \cs{edef} or \cs{expanded} are indicated with a star.

  Most user commands can be safely put into \cs{edef} but then do
  nothing at all (because they are internally protected either
  by \cs{protect} or by being defined with \cs{protected}). Such
  commands are not marked with a star!
  
\end{function}

\section{Command reference}

\pagenumbering{arabic}

Most of what follows is just a list of all commands defined by
the \LaTeX{} kernel, but at this point not documented or sorted.


%===============================================

\subsection{Declaring commands and environments}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Modern commands with extended syntax}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \NewDocumentCommand,
    \RenewDocumentCommand,
    \DeclareDocumentCommand,
    \ProvideDocumentCommand
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewDocumentCommand} \meta{cmd} \Arg{arg spec} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines \meta{cmd} as a robust document command whose arguments are
  described by \meta{arg spec}, e.g., \texttt{m} for a mandatory
  argument, \texttt{o} or \texttt{O\Arg{default}} for an optional
  argument in brackets, \texttt{s} for a star, and so on. Inside
  \meta{code} the arguments are available as \texttt{\#1},
  \texttt{\#2}, etc. The variants differ only in what happens if
  \meta{cmd} is already defined (or not): \cs[no-index]{New\ldots}
  gives an error if it exists, \cs[no-index]{Renew\ldots} gives an
  error if it doesn't, \cs[no-index]{Provide\ldots} silently does
  nothing if it exists, and \cs[no-index]{Declare\ldots} always
  defines it.
  This is the recommended interface for new commands that take
  arguments; for details see \texttt{usrguide}.
\end{function}
\modifiers[NewDocumentCommand]{xparse-2018-04-12, xparse-generic.tex}
\modifiers[RenewDocumentCommand]{xparse-2018-04-12, xparse-generic.tex}
\modifiers[DeclareDocumentCommand]{xparse-2018-04-12,
  xparse-generic.tex}
\modifiers[ProvideDocumentCommand]{xparse-2018-04-12,
  xparse-generic.tex}




\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \NewExpandableDocumentCommand,
    \RenewExpandableDocumentCommand,
    \DeclareExpandableDocumentCommand,
    \ProvideExpandableDocumentCommand
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewExpandableDocumentCommand} \meta{cmd} \Arg{arg spec} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{NewDocumentCommand} and friends, but \meta{cmd} is made
  expandable, so it can be used inside \cs{edef}, \cs{csname}, or
  similar contexts. In return the \meta{arg spec} is restricted: the
  last argument must be mandatory and some types (such as
  verbatim arguments) are not supported. Only use this if expandability
  is really needed.
\end{function}
\modifiers[NewExpandableDocumentCommand]{xparse-2018-04-12,
  xparse-generic.tex}
\modifiers[RenewExpandableDocumentCommand]{xparse-2018-04-12,
  xparse-generic.tex}
\modifiers[DeclareExpandableDocumentCommand]{xparse-2018-04-12,
  xparse-generic.tex}
\modifiers[ProvideExpandableDocumentCommand]{xparse-2018-04-12,
  xparse-generic.tex}



%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Basic command definitions}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \newcommand,
    \renewcommand,
    \providecommand
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newcommand} * \meta{cmd} \oarg{num} \oarg{default} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines \meta{cmd} to take \meta{num} arguments (0--9, default 0),
  referred to as \texttt{\#1}, \ldots, \texttt{\#9} in \meta{code}. If
  \meta{default} is given, the first argument becomes optional (in
  brackets) and \meta{default} is used when it is absent; all further
  arguments are mandatory. \cs{newcommand} gives an error if
  \meta{cmd} is already defined, \cs{renewcommand} if it isn't, and
  \cs{providecommand} makes the definition only if \meta{cmd} is
  undefined.

  Without the star the arguments are \cs{long}, i.e., may contain
  \cs{par}; the starred form produces commands whose arguments can't.
  Commands without arguments are never made \cs{long} (since 2025/11).
  For more complex argument structures use \cs{NewDocumentCommand}.
\end{function}
\modifiers[newcommand]{autoarea, beamerbaseoverlay, colonequals,
  combine, opcit, pdfx, standalone}
\modifiers[renewcommand]{algorithm2e, beamerbaseoverlay, scrbase,
  scrbase-20260202}
\modifiers[providecommand]{revtex4-1, revtex4-2, vncaps.tex}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \CheckCommand
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{CheckCommand} * \meta{cmd} \oarg{num} \oarg{default} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Takes the same arguments as \cs{newcommand} but defines nothing.
  Instead, it checks that \meta{cmd} currently has exactly that
  definition and issues a warning if not. Default values for optional
  arguments are not compared. Useful in packages before redefining a
  kernel or package command, to detect that some other package has
  already changed it. Only usable in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiers{neoschool, pxeverysel}

  Internals for \cs{CheckCommand}: \cs{check@command} grabs the

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@star@or@long
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@star@or@long} \meta{definer}
  \end{syntax}
  Looks ahead for a star, sets \cs{l@ngrel@x} accordingly, resets
  \cs{pr@tectedrel@x} to \cs{relax}, and then calls \meta{definer}
  (e.g., \cs{new@command}). This is how \cs{newcommand} and friends
  implement their star forms.

\end{function}

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \l@ngrel@x,
    \pr@tectedrel@x
  }
  Either \cs{relax} or \cs{long} (respectively \cs{protected}); inserted in
  front of the \cs{def} that \cs{newcommand} and friends finally
  execute. Their values are only meaningful inside the definition
  machinery, so don't set or test them elsewhere.

\end{function}

%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Low-level command definitions}

These are \TeX{} primitives; they are listed here because package
code uses them all the time. Unlike \cs{newcommand} they never check
whether the command already exists.

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \def
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{def} \meta{cmd} \meta{parameter text} \Arg{replacement text}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines \meta{cmd} locally. The \meta{parameter text} consists of
  parameters \texttt{\#1} to \texttt{\#9} (in order), possibly mixed
  with delimiter tokens; e.g., with \texttt{\#1.\#2} as \meta{parameter
  text} the first argument is delimited by a dot. Prefixes \cs{global}, \cs{long}, and \cs{protected} can
  be put in front. The \meta{replacement text} is stored unexpanded.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \edef
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{edef} \meta{cmd} \meta{parameter text} \Arg{replacement text}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{def}, but the \meta{replacement text} is fully expanded at
  definition time. Robust \LaTeX{} commands survive this unchanged, but
  fragile ones may break; if the text can contain arbitrary user input
  use \cs{protected@edef} instead.
\end{function}

  {

  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{xdef} \meta{cmd} \meta{parameter text} \Arg{replacement text}
  \end{syntax}
  Same as \cs{global}\cs{edef}. The \LaTeX{} variant that respects
  \cs{protect} is \cs{protected@xdef}. (There is also the primitive
  \cs{gdef}, the same as \cs{global}\cs{def}.)
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \let
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{let} \meta{cmd} \texttt{=} \meta{token}
  \end{syntax}
  Gives \meta{cmd} the current meaning of \meta{token} (the
  \texttt{=} and one following space are optional). If \meta{token} is
  a macro, \meta{cmd} becomes a copy of it that does not change if
  \meta{token} is later redefined. Note that this doesn't work properly
  for robust commands defined with \cs{DeclareRobustCommand} or with
  an optional argument via \cs{newcommand}; use \cs{NewCommandCopy}
  for them.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \futurelet
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{futurelet} \meta{cmd} \meta{token\textsubscript1} \meta{token\textsubscript2}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets \meta{cmd} to the meaning of \meta{token\textsubscript2} (\`a
  la \cs{let}) and then executes \meta{token\textsubscript1} with
  \meta{token\textsubscript2} still in the input. This is the basis
  for look-ahead commands like \cs{@ifnextchar}, which should normally be
  used instead.
\end{function}
\modifiers{hyperref, pdfnotiz}

%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Modern environments with extended syntax}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \NewDocumentEnvironment,
    \RenewDocumentEnvironment,
    \DeclareDocumentEnvironment
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewDocumentEnvironment} \Arg{name} \Arg{arg spec} \Arg{begin code} \Arg{end code}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines the environment \meta{name} with arguments described by
  \meta{arg spec}, as for \cs{NewDocumentCommand}. The arguments are
  available in both \meta{begin code} and \meta{end code}. A
  \texttt{b} in the \meta{arg spec} grabs the whole environment body
  as an argument. The variants differ in their handling of existing
  definitions, as for the corresponding command declarations
  (\cs{ProvideDocumentEnvironment} also exists).
\end{function}
\modifiers[NewDocumentEnvironment]{xparse-2018-04-12,
  xparse-generic.tex}
\modifiers[RenewDocumentEnvironment]{xparse-2018-04-12,
  xparse-generic.tex}
\modifiers[DeclareDocumentEnvironment]{xparse-2018-04-12,
  xparse-generic.tex}


%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Basic environments}




\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \newenvironment,
    \renewenvironment
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newenvironment} * \Arg{name} \oarg{num} \oarg{default} \Arg{begin code} \Arg{end code}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines the environment \meta{name}; arguments are handled as for
  \cs{newcommand} but are only available in \meta{begin code}. To use
  them in \meta{end code} they have to be saved first (or use
  \cs{NewDocumentEnvironment}). The environment is implemented by the
  commands \cs[no-index]{\meta{name}} and \cs[no-index]{end\meta{name}}, so
  \cs{newenvironment} fails if either already exists.
  \cs{renewenvironment} gives an error if the environment is undefined.
\end{function}
\modifiers[newenvironment]{beamerbaseoverlay, combine, gmdoc}
\modifiers[renewenvironment]{beamerbaseoverlay}




\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \renew@environment
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{renew@environment} \Arg{name} \oarg{num} \oarg{default} \Arg{begin code} \Arg{end code}
  \end{syntax}
  The workhorse behind \cs{renewenvironment} after the star has been
  processed. Use \cs{renewenvironment} instead.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\readers{makecmds}

\subsubsection{Support for modern commands and environments with extended syntax}




\begin{function}[TF,user]
  {
    \IfBoolean
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{IfBooleanTF} \meta{boolean} \Arg{true} \Arg{false}
  \end{syntax}
  Tests if \meta{boolean} is either \cs{BooleanFalse} or
  \cs{BooleanTrue} and selects the corresponding argument for further
  processing.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}

\begin{constant}
  {
    \BooleanFalse,
    \BooleanTrue
  }
  The values passed by document command parsers for argument types
  \texttt{s} and \texttt{t} (star or token present or not). They
  should only be tested with \cs{IfBooleanTF}, never by comparing them
  directly.
\end{constant}

%===============================================

\subsection{\LaTeX{} counters and lengths commands}

%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{\LaTeX{} counters}

Each \LaTeX{} counter \meta{name} has a corresponding \TeX{} counter
register (defined internally with \cs{newcount}) with the name
\cs{c@\meta{name}}. All counter assignments are global.

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \newcounter
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newcounter} \Arg{name} \oarg{within}
  \end{syntax}
  Allocates a new \LaTeX{} counter \meta{name}, initialized to zero,
  together with \cs{the\meta{name}} (defined as
  \cs{arabic}\Arg{name}) and an empty \cs{p@\meta{name}} used as a
  prefix by \cs{ref}. Gives an error if the counter already exists. If
  \meta{within} is given, \meta{name} is reset to zero whenever
  \meta{within} is stepped by \cs{stepcounter} or
  \cs{refstepcounter}. Unlike \cs{counterwithin}, this doesn't change
  \cs{the\meta{name}}. Counters are always global.
\end{function}
\modifiers{cleanthesis}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \setcounter,
    \addtocounter,
    \stepcounter
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{setcounter} \Arg{name} \Arg{integer}
    \cs{addtocounter} \Arg{name} \Arg{integer}
    \cs{stepcounter} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Set the counter \meta{name} to \meta{integer}, add \meta{integer}
  to it, or increment it by one. \cs{stepcounter} also resets all
  counters declared to be reset within \meta{name} (via the optional
  argument of \cs{newcounter} or \cs{counterwithin}). \meta{integer}
  can be anything \TeX{} accepts as a number, e.g., \cs{value}\Arg{other}.
  An undefined counter gives an error. The name \texttt{*} denotes the
  current counter, i.e., the one stored in \cs{@currentcounter}.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \refstepcounter
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{refstepcounter} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{stepcounter}, but in addition makes \meta{name} the current
  counter (\cs{@currentcounter}), sets \cs{@currentlabel} to
  \cs{p@\meta{name}}\cs{the\meta{name}} so that a following \cs{label}
  refers to it, and sets a link target (used by \pkg{hyperref} and
  tagging) via the socket \texttt{refstepcounter/target}.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[user,EXP]
  {
    \value
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{value}\Arg{counter}
  \end{syntax}
  Returns the internal counter register \cs{c@\meta{counter}}, so it can
  be used wherever \TeX{} expects a number, e.g., in
  \cs{setcounter}, \cs{ifnum}, or \cs{numexpr}. It does not
  typeset anything; use \cs{the}\cs{value}\Arg{counter} or
  \cs{arabic}\Arg{counter} for that.
\end{function}

  enumitem, xifthen}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \counterwithin,
    \counterwithout
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{counterwithin} * \oarg{format-cmd} \Arg{counter} \Arg{parent-counter}
    \cs{counterwithout} * \oarg{format-cmd} \Arg{counter} \Arg{parent-counter}
  \end{syntax}
  The operation that defines that one counter is reset whenever
  another counter is stepped is also available as the command
  \cs{counterwithin}. In contrast to \cs{newcounter}, it alters
  \cs{the\meta{counter}} to typeset
  \cs{the\meta{parent-counter}}\texttt{.}\meta{format-cmd}\texttt{\{\meta{counter}\}}
  where \meta{format-cmd} is a command such as \cs{roman}. If the
  optional argument is not present, it defaults to \cs{arabic}.

  When using the starred form \cs{the\meta{counter}} is not touched,
  which is useful if it needs a more complex definition or is already
  correctly set up. Obviously, in that case the optional argument is
  meaningless and is ignored if given.

  The \cs{counterwithout} command implements the opposite operation;
  without star it sets \cs{the\meta{counter}} to
  \meta{format-cmd}\texttt{\{\meta{counter}\}}.
\end{function}

\subsubsection{\LaTeX{} lengths}

\LaTeX{} doesn't distinguishes between skips (variabl lengths) and
dimens (fixed lengths), the high-level user commands only provide
skips (called \enquote{lengths} in the \LaTeX{} manual.

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \newlength
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newlength} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Allocates a new skip register as \meta{cmd}, initialized to
  \texttt{0pt}. Gives an error if \meta{cmd} is already defined.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \setlength,
    \addtolength
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{setlength} \meta{cmd} \Arg{length}
    \cs{addtolength} \meta{cmd} \Arg{length}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the length register \meta{cmd} to \meta{length}, or adds
  \meta{length} to it. \meta{cmd} can be any \TeX{} skip or dimen
  register (or parameter such as \cs{parindent}). \meta{length} may
  include stretch and shrink components, e.g., \texttt{6pt plus 2pt},
  but only if \meta{cmd} is a skip; for a dimen the \texttt{plus}
  part would end up being typeset. The assignment is
  local, unlike counter assignments.

  With the \pkg{calc} package, \meta{length} can be an arithmetic expression.
\end{function}
\modifiers[setlength]{adjcalc, adjustbox, combinedgraphics, linguho,
  lwarp, realboxes}
\modifiers[addtolength]{adjcalc, lwarp}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \settowidth,
    \settoheight
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{settowidth} \meta{cmd} \Arg{material}
  \end{syntax}
  Typesets \meta{material} in LR-mode in a temporary box (with
  tagging suspended) and sets the length register \meta{cmd} to the
  natural width (respectively height) of the result. The material is
  not output. \cs{settodepth} is the analogue for the depth.
\end{function}
\modifiers[settowidth]{linguho}
\modifiers[settoheight]{olabels}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@settodim
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@settodim} \meta{box dimension} \meta{register} \Arg{material}
  \end{syntax}
  The common implementation of \cs{settowidth} and friends: typesets
  \meta{material} in a temporary box and assigns its
  \meta{box dimension} (\cs{wd}, \cs{ht}, or \cs{dp}) to
  \meta{register}. Normally the user-level commands are preferable.

\end{function}
\modifiers{chronos}
\publicreaders{}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@settopoint
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@settopoint} \meta{skip or dimen register}
  \end{syntax}
   This macro takes the contents of the skip or dimen register that is
   supplied as its argument and removes the fractional part to make
   it a whole number of points. This can be used in class files to
   avoid values like |345.4666666pt| when calculating a dimension.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}

\subsection{Text commands}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ ,
    \space,
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{\space} \cs{\space} \cs{\space}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  The command \verb*=\ = typesets a space character, same as just
  using a \verb*= =, but it can be used in places where a normal space
  gets ignored, e.g., after a command such as \verb*=\LaTeX\ =. Several
  such commands in a row produce multiple spaces in contrast to using
  several normal spaces in a row, e.g., the example above would produce 3
  spaces.

  The \verb*=\ = command is a \TeX{} primitive for typesetting a space
  and for some operations, such as assigning a \cs{catcode} to the
  space character or displaying a space in \cs{typeout} one needs to
  use \cs{\space} to refer to this character.

  The command \cs{space} is a command that contains a space character
  as its replacement material. For typesetting this is identical to
  using \verb*=\ = but in other cases there are differences:
  \cs{csname}\texttt{ X}\cs{space}\cs{endcsname} produces a macro name with a space
  character in the name. In that position \cs{\space} (as a
  typesetting instruction) would not be allowed. For the same reason
  you need to use \cs{space} and not \cs{\space} inside \cs{typeout}.

\end{function}
\modifiers[space]{fancyheadings, hyperref, listings, lstmisc, ltb2bib,
  microtype, msg, pgfmanual.pdflinks.code.tex, skeyval-ltxcmds.tex}

\subsubsection{Text accents}

\begin{function}[user,EXP]
  {
    \",
    \',
    \.,
    \~,
    \b,
    \c,
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{"}\meta{base letter}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  These commands typeset various diacritics. These days \LaTeX{} is
  fully Unicode-aware (even in 8-bit engines like \pdfTeX{}) so that
  one normally simply writes \texttt{ä} instead of \cs{"}\texttt{a} (or even
  \cs{"}\texttt{\{a\}} as it was recommended in Lamport's manual).

  However, this remains a valid input syntax and it makes it possible
  to even produce glyphs not part of Unicode, e.g., \"\$ (produced
  with \cs{"}\cs{\$}). If the current font encoding has a precomposed
  glyph it is used, otherwise the accent is placed over the base
  letter.

\end{function}

\subsubsection{Text characters and symbols}

These days characters and symbols can be entered directly as UTF-8
encoded characters (and typeset if the used font supports them). Many
of them are also available via command names, largely for historical
reasons, when \TeX{} was still 8-bit based. In certain situations these
are still useful, for example, if your keyboard doesn't allow you
easily to produce a certain Unicode character.

There are also a few that need command names because they serve as
syntax characters in \TeX{}.

\begin{function}[user,EXP]
  {
    \$,
    \#,
    \&,
    \textasciitilde
  }
%
  They produce \$, \#, \&; using them directly as characters is not
  easily possible as they have syntax functions. For
  \textasciitilde\ one needs to use the long command name, because
  \cs{~} is used for a tilde accent.

  There is also \cs{\%} for a percent sign (without the backslash it
  would start a line comment). Due to some limitation of the macros we
  use here it can't be displayed in the syntax box.

\end{function}
\modifiers[textasciitilde]{aastex701, drm, hyperref, ltxutil, lwarp,
  revtex4-1, revtex4-2}

%\begin{function}[]
%  {
%    \%

\subsubsection{Text emphasis}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \emph,
    \strongemph
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{emph}  \Arg{text}
    \cs{strongemph}  \Arg{text}
  \end{syntax}
  Mark \meta{text} as emphasized text or strongly emphasized
  text. Rendering depends on configuration. \cs{emph} usually
  alternates between italics and normal shape, \cs{strongemph}
  typically uses bold face. Configurable through declarations
  \cs{DeclareEmphSequence} and \cs{DeclareStrongEmphSequence}.
  The corresponding declarations are \cs{em} and \cs{strongem}.
\end{function}

  biblatex2bibitem, blog, datagidx, datagidx-2019-09-27, euproposal,
  exam-n, examdesign, figbib, glossaries-extra,
  glossaries-extra-2021-11-22, hardwrap, hpsdiss, huaz, hyperref,
  l8ulat-penc.def, linguistix-languages, linguistix-malayalam,
  linguistix-marathi, lwarp, manuscript, missaali, njuthesis-doc,
  pdfnotiz, pdfwin, quantumview, reledmac, revtex4-1, revtex4-2,
  skrapport, spimbasephdthesis, talk-simple, tudscrmanual, yb-book,
  zugferd}
\modifiers[strongemph]{}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareEmphSequence,
    \DeclareStrongEmphSequence
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareEmphSequence} \Arg{list of font changes}
  \end{syntax}
  The \meta{list of font changes} is a comma separated list whose
  entries are used when \cs{emph} is called (later entries are used if
  \cs{emph} is nested). An entry is skipped if it doesn't change the
  current font (unless it contains \cs{emforce}). If the nesting is
  deeper than available entries \cs{emreset} is used after the last
  entry and then the sequence is repeated. The declarations are
  additive, e.g.,
  \begin{alltt}
    \cs{DeclareEmphSequence}\{\cs{itshape},\cs{upshape}\cs{scshape},\cs{itshape}\}
  \end{alltt}

  \cs{DeclareStrongEmphSequence} provides the same for \cs{strongemph}.

\end{function}
\modifiers[DeclareEmphSequence]{}
\modifiers[DeclareStrongEmphSequence]{}
\publicreaders[DeclareEmphSequence]{fduthesis, fontspec-luatex,
  fontspec-xetex, nwafupaper, nwafuthesis, rwth-fonts}
\publicreaders[DeclareStrongEmphSequence]{}

  model).
\end{variable}

\begin{function}[user]

  }

  \end{syntax}
  Used inside an entry of \cs{DeclareEmphSequence}
  (respectively \cs{DeclareStrongEmphSequence}) to force the use of

\end{function}
\modifiers[emforce]{}
\modifiers[strongemforce]{}




\begin{function}[user]

  \end{syntax}

\subsubsection{Math environments}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \(,
    \)
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{(} \meta{inline math} \cs{)}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  \LaTeX's alternative to \verb=$...$= for inline formulas. \cs{(}
  gives an error if already in math mode and \cs{)} if not, so
  mismatched delimiters are detected, but many authors prefer
  \verb=$...$= as it is easier to read in the source.
\end{function}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \[,
    \]
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{[} \meta{display math} \cs{]}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  \LaTeX's short commands for unnumbered display formulas, same as the
  \texttt{displaymath} environment. It is not equivalent to the plain
  \TeX{} syntax \verb=$$...$$=, which does not work correctly with
  several \LaTeX{} features (e.g., \texttt{fleqn}, tagging) and should
  not be used in a \LaTeX{} document!
\end{function}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \math,
    \endmath
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{begin}\Arg{math}  \meta{inline math} \cs{end}\Arg{math}
  \end{syntax}
  Long environment form of \cs{(}\ldots\cs{)}.
\end{function}

\subsection{Programming}



%----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Hooks}

It is a bit of a debate which hook commands are user facing. Most are
really meant for packages or classes.  A few are sometimes useful in
the preamble or even in the document body and those have been marked
\enquote{user} but this is at best a rough indication. For details see
the documentation of \texttt{lthooks}.

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewHook,
    \NewReversedHook,
    \NewMirroredHookPair
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewHook} \Arg{hook}
    \cs{NewReversedHook} \Arg{hook}
    \cs{NewMirroredHookPair} \Arg{hook\textsubscript1} \Arg{hook\textsubscript2}
  \end{syntax}
  Declare a new hook, i.e., a named place in the code (executed with
  \cs{UseHook}) to which packages and users can add code with
  \cs{AddToHook}. In a reversed hook the code chunks are executed in
  reverse order, which is useful for \enquote{end} hooks matching a
  \enquote{begin} hook; \cs{NewMirroredHookPair} declares such a pair.
  In package code \meta{hook} can start with \texttt{.}, which is
  replaced by the package name. Hook names must be unique and
  declarations are global.
\end{function}
\modifiers[NewHook]{}
\modifiers[NewReversedHook]{}
\modifiers[NewMirroredHookPair]{}
\publicreaders[NewHook]{csvsimple-l3, easybase, fcolumn-2026-01-16,
  hgbthesis, huaz, hyperref, incgraph, jsmembertable,
  latex-lab-testphase-bookmark, memoir, postnotes, robust-externalize,
  scrartcl, scrbook, scrreprt, sjtu-lang-de.def, sjtu-lang-en.def,
  sjtu-lang-ja.def, sjtu-lang-zh.def, sjtu-thesis-preset-base.def,
  tikzducks, tikzlings, tikzlings-anteaters, tikzlings-apes,
  tikzlings-bats, tikzlings-bears, tikzlings-bees, tikzlings-bugs,
  tikzlings-cats, tikzlings-chickens, tikzlings-coatis, tikzlings-dogs,
  tikzlings-elephants, tikzlings-hippos, tikzlings-koalas,
  tikzlings-marmots, tikzlings-meerkats, tikzlings-mice,
  tikzlings-moles, tikzlings-owls, tikzlings-pandas, tikzlings-penguins,
  tikzlings-pigs, tikzlings-rhinos, tikzlings-sheep, tikzlings-sloths,
  tikzlings-snowmen, tikzlings-squirrels, tikzlings-turkeys,
  tikzlings-wolves, zref-clever}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewHookWithArguments,
    \NewReversedHookWithArguments,
    \NewMirroredHookPairWithArguments
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewHookWithArguments} \Arg{hook} \Arg{number}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{NewHook} and friends but the hook takes \meta{number}
  arguments (1--9). They have to be provided by
  \cs{UseHookWithArguments} and can be accessed as \texttt{\#1},
  \ldots{} in code added with \cs{AddToHookWithArguments}.
\end{function}

\modifiers[NewReversedHookWithArguments]{}
\modifiers[NewMirroredHookPairWithArguments]{}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \AddToHook
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{AddToHook} \Arg{hook} \oarg{label} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Adds \meta{code} to \meta{hook} under the name \meta{label}
  (default: the current package name, or \texttt{top-level} in the
  document). Code with different labels can be ordered with
  \cs{DeclareHookRule}. The hook need not exist yet; generic hooks
  such as \texttt{env/\meta{env}/begin}, \texttt{cmd/\meta{cmd}/before}, or
  \texttt{file/\meta{file}/after} are created on the fly. A \texttt{\#}
  in \meta{code} must be doubled if the hook takes arguments; use
  \cs{AddToHookWithArguments} in that case. Additions are global.
\end{function}
\modifiers{unhook.tex}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \AddToHookNext
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{AddToHookNext} \Arg{hook} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Adds \meta{code} to the next execution of \meta{hook} only; it is
  executed after the normal hook code and then discarded. Code added
  this way can't be ordered by rules.
\end{function}
\modifiers{unhook.tex}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \AddToHookWithArguments,
    \AddToHookNextWithArguments
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{AddToHookWithArguments} \Arg{hook} \oarg{label} \Arg{code}
    \cs{AddToHookNextWithArguments} \Arg{hook} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Variants of \cs{AddToHook} and \cs{AddToHookNext} for hooks with
  arguments, where \texttt{\#1}, \ldots{} in \meta{code} refer to the
  hook arguments (and a literal \texttt{\#} must be doubled).
\end{function}
\modifiers[AddToHookWithArguments]{unhook.tex}
\modifiers[AddToHookNextWithArguments]{unhook.tex}





\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ActivateGenericHook

  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ActivateGenericHook} \Arg{hook}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares \meta{hook} as a generic hook that a package provides
  (executed with \cs{UseHook}) but that is not declared with
  \cs{NewHook}, typically because only some instances of a family
  of hooks are needed. Does nothing if the hook is already activated.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DisableGenericHook
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DisableGenericHook} \Arg{hook}
  \end{syntax}
  Disables the generic \meta{hook} so that code can no longer be added
  to it (an error is given). Use this, for example, if an environment
  or command implements the hook explicitly and generic hook code
  would never be executed.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\publicreaders{}




\begin{function}[]
  {
    \UseHook
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{UseHook} \Arg{hook}
  \end{syntax}
  Executes the code stored in \meta{hook} (in the order determined by
  the hook rules) followed by any \enquote{next} code. Does nothing if
  the hook is empty or undeclared. Package code should normally use it
  only for hooks it has declared itself.
\end{function}

\subsubsection{Sockets}

Sockets are named places in the code whose behavior is determined by
an assigned \enquote{plug}, so that different implementations (e.g.,
with and without tagging) can be switched in and out. For details see
the documentation of \texttt{ltsockets}.

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewSocket
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewSocket} \Arg{socket} \Arg{number of inputs}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares a new socket that expects \meta{number of inputs}
  arguments. It automatically gets a plug \texttt{noop}, which
  removes the inputs; sockets with one input also get the plug
  \texttt{identity} (returning the input unchanged), which is then
  the default. Only allowed at top level, not in a group.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\publicreaders{gia-handout, hyperref, sillypage}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \UseSocket
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{UseSocket} \Arg{socket} \meta{inputs}
  \end{syntax}
  Executes the plug currently assigned to \meta{socket}, passing it
  the \meta{inputs} (as many brace groups as declared). For
  performance reasons there is no check that the socket exists.
\end{function}
\modifiers{unhook.tex}
\publicreaders{cuted, hyperref}




\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewSocketPlug
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewSocketPlug}  \Arg{socket}  \Arg{plug} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares \meta{plug} for \meta{socket}: \meta{code} is executed when
  the plug is assigned and the socket is used, with the socket inputs
  available as \texttt{\#1}, \texttt{\#2}, \ldots. Gives an error if
  the plug already exists. The declaration is local.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\publicreaders{asmeconf, asmejour, footmisc, gia-handout, hyperref,
  l3backend-pdf-luatex.def, l3backend-testphase-luatex.def, ltx-talk,
  moloch-talk, sblarticle, sblbook, sblreport, scrartcl, scrbook,
  scrreprt, sillypage}

  {
    \AssignSocketPlug
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{AssignSocketPlug} \Arg{socket} \Arg{plug}
  \end{syntax}
  Makes \meta{plug} the active plug for \meta{socket}. Gives an error
  if either doesn't exist. The assignment is local.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}

\subsubsection{Low-level programming}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@namedef
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@namedef}\Arg{name}\meta{parameter text}\Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Equivalent to \cs{def}\cs[no-index]{\meta{name}}\meta{parameter
  text}\Arg{code}, but the command name is given as a string, which is
  expanded inside \cs{csname}, e.g.,
  \begin{alltt}
    \cs{@namedef}\{ver@\#1.sty\}\{\meta{date and version}\}
  \end{alltt}
  No check is made whether the command already exists. The definition
  is local.

\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@cons
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@cons} \meta{list cmd} \Arg{item}
  \end{syntax}
  Appends \cs{@elt}\,\meta{item} globally to \meta{list cmd}. The
  \meta{item} is expanded with \cs{edef} (except for \cs{@elt}), so
  it normally should be a single command or protected material. Lists
  of this form, e.g., \cs{cl@\meta{counter}}, are processed by locally
  defining \cs{@elt} and then executing the \meta{list cmd}.

\end{function}
\modifiers{locality, scrlayer}
\publicreaders{aastex701, aliasctr, altxext, beamerbaseframe, bicaption,
  bigfoot, caption3, caption3\_2010-01-14, caption3\_2011-11-01,

\begin{function}[EXP]
  {
    \@car,
    \@cdr,
    \@carcube
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@car} \meta{item\textsubscript1} \meta{items} \cs{@nil}
    \cs{@cdr} \meta{item\textsubscript1} \meta{items} \cs{@nil}
    \cs{@carcube} \meta{item\textsubscript1} \meta{item\textsubscript2} \meta{item\textsubscript3} \meta{items} \cs{@nil}
  \end{syntax}
  List operations (named after their Lisp counterparts) on the
  material up to \cs{@nil}, where an \meta{item} is a single token or
  a brace group. \cs{@car} returns \meta{item\textsubscript1} (with
  braces removed) and drops the rest, \cs{@cdr} drops
  \meta{item\textsubscript1} and returns the remaining \meta{items},
  and \cs{@carcube} returns the first three items (with braces
  removed) and drops the rest. For example,
  \begin{alltt}
    \cs{@car} abc\cs{@nil} \textyields{} a
    \cs{@cdr} abc\cs{@nil} \textyields{} bc
  \end{alltt}
  The material must contain at least one item (\cs{@carcube}: four).
  \cs{@car} and \cs{@cdr} are not \cs{long}, so the material must not
  contain \cs{par}.

\end{function}

\modifiers[@cdr]{nath}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@gobble,

  \begin{syntax}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \zap@space
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{zap@space} \meta{material} \verb*/ /\cs{@empty}
  \end{syntax}
  Removes all spaces (at the top level, i.e., not inside braces) from
  \meta{material}. It grabs everything up to the first space, returns
  it and drops the space. Then it checks if the token after the space
  was \cs{@empty}. If yes, it stops processing, otherwise it
  recursively calls itself on the rest of \meta{material}. Usually
  used inside an \cs{edef}, e.g., to clean up a comma separated list.

  For this to work the \meta{material} is not allowed to contain
  \verb*/ /\cs{@empty}.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \ifnot@nil
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ifnot@nil} \Arg{test code} \Arg{true code}
  \end{syntax}
  If \meta{test code} is not the token \cs{@nnil} (compared via a
  scratch macro with \cs{ifx}), executes \meta{true code}, otherwise
  removes it. Despite its name it tests for \cs{@nnil} and not
  \cs{@nil}.
\end{function}

\begin{constant}
  {
    \@nnil
  }
%
  Macro that serves as a delimiter in constructions with delimited
  arguments and as an end marker in lists, e.g.,
  \begin{alltt}
    \cs{@defaultunits}\cs{@tempdimb} \#5pt\cs{relax}\cs{@nnil}
  \end{alltt}
  It expands to the undefined \cs{@nil}, so it must never be
  executed; loops such as \cs{@for} compare an item with it using
  \cs{ifx} to detect the end (see also \cs{ifnot@nil}). \cs{@nil}
  itself is used only as an argument delimiter.
\end{constant}

\begin{constant}
  {
    \@empty
  }
%
  A macro that expands to nothing. Can be used, for example, to test
  with \cs{ifx} if a macro replacement text is empty. The definition
  is not \cs{long} which is an important restriction in such tests: a
  \cs{long} macro with empty replacement text is not \cs{ifx}-equal to
  \cs{@empty}.
\end{constant}

%----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Loops}

For new code the L3 programming layer offers much better loop
constructs (e.g., \texttt{\textbackslash clist\_map\_inline:nn}); the
loops below are mostly of interest for reading existing code.

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@whilenum
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@whilenum} \meta{\TeX{} boolean expression} \cs{do} \Arg{loop body}
  \end{syntax}
  \meta{\TeX{} boolean expression} is an expression that can follow
  after \cs{ifnum}, e.g., \cs{@tempcnta}\texttt{>5}. While the
  condition is true \meta{loop body} is executed which is supposed to
  alter the condition eventually, e.g., by changing \cs{@tempcnta} in
  this example. The loop is not executed in a group.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}

\begin{function}[]

    \@whiledim
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@whiledim} \meta{\TeX{} boolean expression} \cs{do} \Arg{loop body}
  \end{syntax}
  Same as \cs{@whilenum} but for expressions following \cs{ifdim}.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@whilesw
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@whilesw} \meta{\TeX{} \enquote{if} conditional} \cs{fi} \Arg{loop body}
  \end{syntax}
  While \meta{\TeX{} \enquote{if} conditional}, e.g.,
  \cs{if@tempswa}, is true execute \meta{loop body}, which needs to
  set it to false at some point to exit the loop.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@for
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@for} \meta{cmd} := \meta{comma list} \cs{do} \Arg{loop body}
  \end{syntax}
  Executes \meta{loop body} for each item of \meta{comma list}, with
  \meta{cmd} defined (locally, via \cs{def}) to the current item. The
  \meta{comma list} is expanded once, so it can be a macro holding the
  list. Spaces around items are not removed and empty items are
  processed. Afterwards the loop variable is \cs{ifx}-equal to \cs{@nnil}.

  Does not work in code where \cs{ExplSyntaxOn} is active because
  there \texttt{:} has a different \cs{catcode}.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@tfor
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@tfor} \meta{cmd} := \meta{tokens} \cs{do} \Arg{loop body}
  \end{syntax}
  Loops over all items in \meta{tokens} (single tokens or brace groups;
  spaces are skipped) and defines \meta{cmd} to contain the next
  item and then processes the \meta{loop body} until it runs out of
  items or \cs{@break@tfor} is seen in the \meta{loop body}. Unlike
  \cs{@for}, the \meta{tokens} are not expanded.

  The L3 programming layer has much better functions for such
  programming tasks!
\end{function}
\modifiers{}

%----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Catcode manipulations}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \makeatletter,
    \makeatother
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{makeatletter} \meta{material} \cs{makeatother}
  \end{syntax}
  Set the catcode of the \texttt{@}-sign to \enquote{letter}
  (respectively back to \enquote{other}) so that internal \LaTeXe{}
  commands can be accessed, e.g., in the document preamble. Not
  needed in package and class files where \texttt{@} is a letter
  anyway. Note that catcodes are fixed when text is read, so this
  doesn't work inside an argument of another command.
\end{function}
\modifiers[makeatletter]{arabtex.tex, bussproofs, chess, poemscol,
  skdoc}
\modifiers[makeatother]{arabtex.tex, at, bussproofs, poemscol, tvz-hax}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ExplSyntaxOn,
    \ExplSyntaxOff
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ExplSyntaxOn} ... \cs{ExplSyntaxOff}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets up the programming conventions for the L3 programming layer,
  e.g., spaces are ignored and \texttt{\_} and \texttt{:} are letters
  so can be used in command names; \texttt{\textasciitilde} produces
  a space. (The \texttt{@}-sign is not altered.)
\end{function}
\modifiers[ExplSyntaxOn]{chextras}
\modifiers[ExplSyntaxOff]{chextras}




\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@sanitize
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{begingroup}\cs{@sanitize} \ldots{} \cs{endgroup}
  \end{syntax}
  Changes the catcodes of all special characters (space,
  \texttt{\textbackslash}, \texttt{\$}, \texttt{\&}, \texttt{\#},
  \texttt{\textasciicircum}, \texttt{\_}, \texttt{\%},
  \texttt{\textasciitilde}) to \enquote{other} (12), but not those of
  braces. Used, e.g., for reading arguments of \cs{index} and
  \cs{glossary} verbatim. The change is local, so it should be used
  inside a group.
\end{function}
\modifiers{amsldoc, at, fancyvrb, gmverb, gmverse, listings,
  sanitize-umlaut, syntax, xdoc2}

\subsubsection{Generating errors, warnings, and info messages}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \PackageError
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{PackageError}\Arg{package}\Arg{message}\Arg{help message}
  \end{syntax}
  Generates an error message for package \meta{package} displaying
  \meta{message} on the terminal introduced by \texttt{Package
    \meta{package} Error:}.  Processing is stopped and awaits a
  reaction from the user. If the user replies with pressing \texttt{h}
  the \meta{help message} is shown as well.

  Inside \meta{message} the command \cs{MessageBreak} can be used to
  produce suitable line breaks to structure the message.  Displaying
  and formatting the error message is done using \cs{GenericError}
  internally.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \PackageWarning,
    \PackageWarningNoLine,
    \PackageNote,
    \PackageNoteNoLine,
    \PackageInfo,
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{PackageWarning}\Arg{package}\Arg{message}
  \end{syntax}
  Generates a package warning on the terminal (with or without
  displaying the current line number). The \meta{message} is preceded
  by \texttt{Package \meta{package} Warning:}. The command
  \cs{MessageBreak} can be used to produce suitable line breaks to
  structure the message.  Displaying and formatting the warning
  message is done using \cs{GenericWarning} internally.

  The commands \cs{PackageNote} and \cs{PackageNoteNoLine} only differ
  in that they use \texttt{Package \meta{package} Info:} at the
  beginning, i.e., they show their \meta{message} on the terminal but
  not as a warning; instead they offer \enquote{information} of some
  kind.

  The command \cs{PackageInfo} is like \cs{PackageNote} but writes its
  \meta{message} only to the transcript and not to the terminal.
\end{function}
\modifiers[PackageWarning]{gmbase, letterspace, msg, olabels, silence,
  skeyval-ltxcmds.tex}
\modifiers[PackageWarningNoLine]{silence, skeyval-ltxcmds.tex,
  tudscrartcl, tudscrbook, tudscrposter, tudscrreprt}
\modifiers[PackageNote]{}
\modifiers[PackageNoteNoLine]{}
\modifiers[PackageInfo]{skeyval-ltxcmds.tex}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \MessageBreak
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{PackageWarning}\Arg{package}\{\meta{text}\cs{MessageBreak}\meta{more text}\}
  \end{syntax}
  Starts a new line inside the message of \cs{PackageError},
  \cs{PackageWarning}, etc., indented and prefixed so that it lines up
  with the first line (e.g., with \texttt{(\meta{package})}). Outside
  such messages it is \cs{relax}.
\end{function}

\begin{variable}[user]
  {
    \c@errorcontextlines
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{setcounter}\texttt{\{errorcontextlines\}\{100\}}
  \end{syntax}
  \LaTeX{} counter that defines how many lines from the macro
  processing stack are shown when an error occurs. Default value is
  \texttt{-1} as they are usually not helpful for most users. But if
  one needs to see the context it can be useful to set it to a high
  enough number.
\end{variable}
\setters{dtk, moredefs, texpower, tikz-kalender}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \GenericError
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{GenericError} \Arg{continuation} \Arg{message} \Arg{explanation} \Arg{help}
  \end{syntax}
  The basis for all \LaTeX{} error messages. Displays \meta{message}
  (where \cs{MessageBreak} starts a new line beginning with
  \meta{continuation}) followed by \meta{explanation} (e.g., a
  reference to the documentation) and stops; \meta{help} is shown if
  the user types \texttt{h}. In packages and classes use
  \cs{PackageError} or \cs{ClassError} instead.
\end{function}

  skeyval-ltxcmds.tex, srdp-tables, tabu}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \GenericInfo,
    \GenericWarning
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{GenericInfo}\Arg{continuation}\Arg{message}
  \end{syntax}
  The basis for all \LaTeX{} warnings and info messages, with
  \meta{continuation} used after each \cs{MessageBreak}.
  \cs{GenericWarning} writes to the terminal and the transcript file,
  \cs{GenericInfo} only to the latter.
\end{function}
\modifiers[GenericInfo]{hyperref, pdfnotiz, skeyval-ltxcmds.tex}

  skeyval-ltxcmds.tex}

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@latex@error,
    \@latex@warning,
    \@latex@warning@no@line,
    \@latex@note,
    \@latex@note@no@line
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@latex@error} \Arg{message} \Arg{help text}
    \cs{@latex@warning} \Arg{message}
  \end{syntax}
  Error, warning or info messages for use in the \LaTeX{} kernel. They
  announce themselves as \texttt{LaTeX Error:}, \texttt{LaTeX Warning:},
  or \texttt{LaTeX Info:}.

  They should normally only be used by the kernel, i.e., not in
  package or classes. There, one should use \cs{PackageError},
  \cs{ClassWarning}, etc.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[int,deprecated]
  {
    \@latexbug
  }
  %
  This command generates an error that claims that there may be a bug
  in \LaTeX{} itself. While that is quite possible it is something
  that should not be claimed in any package or class code. Thus this
  command \textbf{should not be used} anywhere and eventually it will
  get also removed from the two places it is still used in the kernel
  (because it is essentially nonsense there).

\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@eha,
    \@ehb,
    \@ehc,
    \@ehd
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@latex@error}\{Unknown symbol font `\#2'\}\cs{@eha}
  \end{syntax}
  Simple fixed help texts for error messages used together with \cs{@latex@error} as shown in the example.

  \cs{@eha} gives \texttt{Your command was ignored. Type ...}

  \cs{@ehb} gives \texttt{You've lost some text. \cs{@ehc}}

  \cs{@ehc} gives \texttt{Try typing <return> to proceed. If that doesn't work ...}

  \cs{@ehd} gives the lovely \texttt{You're in trouble here. \cs{@ehc}}
\end{function}

  fixed \meta{message} and one of the \cs{@eha}, \cs{@ehb}, or
  \cs{@ehd} help texts, e.g., \cs{@badend} produces the error message
  \begin{quote}\ttfamily

  \end{quote}

  from the days of \LaTeX\,2.09). Most of the time \cs{@latex@error} is
  used directly in the code.

\end{function}

\subsubsection{Scratch registers and macros}

their value is only reliable between commands you control. They
should only be set locally.

%===============================================

\subsection{Font handling in \LaTeX{} (NFSS)}

In NFSS a font is described by five attributes: encoding, family,
series, shape, and size. For details see \texttt{fntguide}.

\subsubsection{Declarations for text and math fonts}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontShape
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontShape} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape} \Arg{size specs} \Arg{special}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares which external fonts to use for the given combination of
  attributes at which sizes. \meta{size specs} is a list of entries
  such as \texttt{<10> cmr10} or \texttt{<->s*[0.95] fontname},
  possibly using size functions like \texttt{sub} or \texttt{ssub}
  for substitutions. \meta{special} is code executed each time the
  font is loaded (often empty). Usually found in \texttt{.fd} files;
  the \meta{family} must have been declared with \cs{DeclareFontFamily}.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}




\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFixedFont
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFixedFont} \meta{cmd} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape} \Arg{size}
  \end{syntax}
  Defines \meta{cmd} as a fast switch to one fixed font, bypassing
  the NFSS selection mechanism. Useful for fonts used often in a fixed
  size (e.g., in headers); \meta{cmd} doesn't update
  \cs{baselineskip}, math fonts, or the current font attributes.
\end{function}
\modifiers{fix-tudscrfonts}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontFamily
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontFamily} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{special}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares \meta{family} in \meta{encoding}. The \meta{special} code
  is executed when any font of the family is loaded, typically to set
  \cs{hyphenchar} or \cs{skewchar}. Usually the first declaration in
  an \texttt{.fd} file.
\end{function}
\modifiers{ctex-engine-pdftex.def}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontFamilySubstitution
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontFamilySubstitution} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{substitution}
  \end{syntax}
  Attempts to load \texttt{.fd} files for \meta{family} and the
  \meta{substitution} family in \meta{encoding} if not loaded already
  and then substitutes all kind of standard shapes from the
  \meta{substitution} family to \meta{family}. This means that from
  that point onwards a request for a shape in \meta{family} will
  always use the shape from \meta{substitution}.

  The substitution is done with \texttt{ssub}, i.e., silently and only
  recorded in the \texttt{.log} file.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \DeclareErrorFont
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareErrorFont} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape} \Arg{size}
  \end{syntax}
  For a fully functional NFSS setup there has to be one
  \cs{DeclareErrorFont} declaration for each \meta{encoding} known to
  NFSS. Its purpose is to select this font shape when a requested font
  shape can't be found and the automatic substitution
  mechanism also doesn't lead to an existing font.

  This declaration should only be used by the kernel or by the few
  packages that provide additional \meta{encoding}s for \LaTeX. It
  \emph{should not} be used by packages that provide additional fonts,
  which is why it is marked as internal in this document!

  Only available in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiers{bxjsarticle, bxjsbook, bxjsreport, bxjsslide}
\readers{arabic.ldf, eu1enc.def, eu2enc.def, farsi.ldf, laeenc.def,
  lfeenc.def, lgienc.def, ly1enc.def, mlltxchg.def}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontEncoding
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontEncoding} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{text settings} \Arg{math settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares a new font encoding. \meta{text settings} is executed each
  time the encoding is selected in text, \meta{math settings} when it
  is used for a math alphabet. The commands for the encoding-specific
  glyphs are declared separately (e.g., in an \texttt{\meta{enc}enc.def}
  file) and loaded with \pkg{fontenc}. Only available in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \noaccents@
  }
  Used as \meta{math settings} of encodings (such as \texttt{U})
  without accents. Empty in the kernel; \pkg{amsmath} defines it to
  mark math accents as not available.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\readers{libertinust1math, stix, stix2}





\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \LastDeclaredEncoding
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareTextSymbol}\Arg{cmd}\cs{LastDeclaredEncoding}\Arg{slot}
  \end{syntax}
  Holds the name of the encoding last declared with
  \cs{DeclareFontEncoding}, so that encoding definition files can use
  it in subsequent declarations instead of hard-wiring the name.
\end{function}
\modifiers{mathtext, pdfx, puenc-greek.def, tuenc-greek.def}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontSubstitution
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontSubstitution} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the default font shape for \meta{encoding} that is used as the
  last resort when automatic font substitution doesn't find the
  requested shape. These fonts must exist (at least in one size),
  which is checked at \cs{begin}\texttt{\{document\}}. Only available
  in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}




\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontEncodingDefaults
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontEncodingDefaults} \Arg{text settings} \Arg{math settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares code executed for every encoding in addition to the
  encoding's own settings (stored in \cs{default@T} and
  \cs{default@M}). Use \cs{relax} for an argument that should not
  be changed. Only available in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareEncodingSubset
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareEncodingSubset} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{subset}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares that \meta{family} supports only a subset of
  \meta{encoding} (currently only used for \texttt{TS1}).
  \meta{subset} ranges from \texttt{0} (all glyphs available) to
  \texttt{9} (many missing). A \meta{family} ending in \texttt{-*}
  covers the common variants such as \texttt{-LF} and
  \texttt{-OsF}. Usually placed in \texttt{.fd} files.
\end{function}
\modifiers{nfssext-cfr}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \CheckEncodingSubset
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{CheckEncodingSubset} \meta{use cmd} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{fallback} \Arg{subset} \meta{symbol}
  \end{syntax}
  Used in definitions of text symbols: if the current family supports
  \meta{symbol} (i.e., its declared subset of \meta{encoding} is
  lower than \meta{subset}), executes \meta{use cmd}
  (\cs{UseTextSymbol} or \cs{UseTextAccent})\Arg{encoding}\meta{symbol};
  otherwise \meta{fallback}\meta{symbol}, e.g., an error or a faked
  glyph. See \texttt{lttextcomp.dtx} for examples.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclarePreloadSizes
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclarePreloadSizes} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family} \Arg{series} \Arg{shape} \Arg{size list}
  \end{syntax}
  Loads the given font shape in the sizes of the comma separated
  \meta{size list} already at format generation or in the preamble.
  Rarely needed these days. Only available in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}




\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \LoadFontDefinitionFile
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{LoadFontDefinitionFile} \Arg{encoding} \Arg{family}
  \end{syntax}
  Attempts to load the font definition file (\texttt{.fd}) for the font
  \meta{family} in a specific \meta{encoding}, unless it has already
  been loaded.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \do@subst@correction
  }
  Internal helper for font loading: after a font substitution it
  makes sure that the font identifier for the requested shape points
  to the font actually loaded, so the substitution is not repeated.
\end{function}
\modifiers{ctex-engine-luatex.def, microtype}
\publicreaders{CJK, anyfontsize}



\begin{constant}
  {
    \cdp@list
  }
  Holds the declared encodings with their substitution
  defaults as a list of
  \cs{cdp@elt}\Arg{encoding}\Arg{family}\Arg{series}\Arg{shape}
  entries. It is built by \cs{DeclareFontEncoding} and
  \cs{DeclareFontSubstitution} and used to check the defaults at
  \cs{begin}\texttt{\{document\}} and whether an encoding has been
  declared. Only available in the preamble.
\end{constant}
\modifiers{mathtext}
\publicreaders{cmsrb, mathfam256, mlltxchg.def, mongolian.ldf,
  unicode-math-luatex, unicode-math-xetex, unicode-persianmath}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \cdp@elt
  }
  Marks an entry in \cs{cdp@list}. It is \cs{relax} and gets
  redefined locally whenever the list is processed.
\end{function}
\modifiers{cmsrb, mathfam256, mathtext, mlltxchg.def, mongolian.ldf}
\publicreaders{unicode-math-luatex, unicode-math-xetex,
  unicode-persianmath}



\begin{constant}
  {
    \default@T,
    \default@M
  }
  Code executed for every encoding in text, respectively math,
  as set by \cs{DeclareFontEncodingDefaults}.
\end{constant}
\modifiers[default@T]{}
\modifiers[default@M]{}
\publicreaders[default@T]{mathtext}
\publicreaders[default@M]{mathtext}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \pickup@font
  }
  Selects the font identifier for the current font attributes, loading
  the font with \cs{define@newfont} if it isn't yet defined. Part of
  \cs{selectfont}.
\end{function}
\modifiers{CJK, CJKutf8, ctex-engine-luatex.def, kotexutf, letterspace,
  microtype}
\publicreaders{bxcjkjatype, everysel-2011-10-28, ltxtools-trace,
  pxeverysel}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \define@newfont
  }
  Loads the font for the current attributes: it loads the \texttt{.fd}
  file if necessary (\cs{try@load@fontshape}), handles substitution if
  the shape doesn't exist, and then calls \cs{extract@font}.
\end{function}
\modifiers{exercisebank, ltxtools-trace, savetrees, wordcount.tex}
\publicreaders{CJK, CJKutf8, ctex-engine-luatex.def, dhucs-cmap,
  kotexutf, letterspace, microtype}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \try@load@fontshape
  }
  Loads the \texttt{.fd} file for the current encoding and family if
  that hasn't been attempted yet.
\end{function}
\modifiers{CJK, mlltxchg.def, wordcount.tex}
\publicreaders{amsart, amsbook, amsdtx, amsldoc, amsproc,
  beamerthemeCelestia, figureversions, fontaxes-v1, listings,
  ltxtools-trace, nfssext-cfr-nfss, nfssext-cfr-nnfss}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \extract@font
  }
  Determines the external font for the current shape and size from the
  \cs{DeclareFontShape} information (via \cs{get@external@font}),
  loads it with \cs{font}, and executes the family's and shape's
  \meta{special} code.
\end{function}
\modifiers{bxcjkjatype, cmap, ctex-engine-luatex.def}
\publicreaders{ltxtools-trace}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \get@external@font
  }
  Helper for \cs{extract@font}: evaluates the size specifications
  (running size functions) and stores the external font name in
  \cs{external@font}.
\end{function}
\modifiers{bxjsarticle, bxjsbook, bxjsreport, bxjsslide}
\publicreaders{CJK, cmap, ctex-engine-luatex.def}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \nfss@catcodes
  }
  Sets catcodes of various symbols such that \texttt{.fd} file can be
  loaded and correctly interpreted regardless of the current catcode
  regime in the document. Should be issued in a group for obvious
  reasons.
\end{function}
\modifiers{eu1enc.def, eu2enc.def, listings, mathastext, mlltxchg.def}

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \split@name
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{split@name} \meta{\LaTeX{} font name} \cs{@nil}

  Expects as \meta{\LaTeX{} font name} of the form

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \wrong@fontshape
  }
  Internal helper used during font selection when the requested shape
  is not available: it determines a substitute (first changing the
  shape, then the series, then the family to the encoding defaults),
  records the substitution, and warns.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\readers{ltxtools-trace, nfssext-cfr-nnfss}




\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \@defaultsubs
  }
  Internal macro that is either empty or contains a warning message
  displayed at the end of the run that some font substitutions have
  happened during the run.

  Currently used in some places outside of the kernel (but only
  because the classes overwrite core \LaTeX{} commands rather than
  using hooks!)
\end{function}
\modifiers{pseudo}
\readers{aastex701, combine, ltxutil, revtex4, revtex4-1, revtex4-2}



%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Document-level text font commands}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \fontencoding
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fontencoding} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the encoding attribute for the next \cs{selectfont}. The
  encoding must have been declared (normally by loading \pkg{fontenc}).
\end{function}
\modifiers{huaz, hyperref, mltex, ucshyper, wordcount.tex, zugferd}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \fontfamily
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fontfamily} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the family attribute, e.g., \texttt{cmr} or \texttt{lmss},
  for the next \cs{selectfont}.
\end{function}
\modifiers{huaz, hyperref, wordcount.tex, zugferd}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \fontsize
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{fontsize} \Arg{size} \Arg{baselineskip}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets the size attribute and the \cs{baselineskip} (multiplied by
  \cs{baselinestretch}) for the next \cs{selectfont}. Without unit,
  \texttt{pt} is assumed. Document-level size commands like
  \cs{small} are defined with it.
\end{function}
\modifiers{huaz, hyperref, wordcount.tex, zugferd}




\begin{function}[]
  {
    \linespread
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{linespread} \Arg{factor}
  \end{syntax}
  Sets \cs{baselinestretch} to \meta{factor}, i.e., scales the
  \cs{baselineskip} of all font sizes, taking effect at the next
  \cs{selectfont}. Typically used in the preamble.
\end{function}
\modifiers{wordcount.tex}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareMathSizes
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareMathSizes} * \Arg{text size} \Arg{math text size} \Arg{script size} \Arg{scriptscript size}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares the sizes of the math fonts to be used when the text font
  has \meta{text size}. If \meta{math text size} is empty, no math
  fonts are set up for that size (useful for large headings). The
  star form only declares the sizes if none were declared before. For
  sizes without declaration, the sizes are computed with
  \cs{defaultscriptratio} and \cs{defaultscriptscriptratio}. Only
  available in the preamble.
\end{function}

  Only used in kernel + ams. Replace?
