%===============================================

\subsection{Design}

%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{Templates}

Most of the code for templates is written in the L3 programming layer
and is internal, i.e., the commands start with \texttt{\_\_}. Here we only
describe the public functions. For details see the documentation of
\texttt{lttemplates}.

A \emph{template type} describes an abstract design object (e.g.,
\enquote{sectioning}) and the number of arguments it takes; a
\emph{template} implements a type with a set of keys; an
\emph{instance} is a template with concrete key values that can be
used in code.


\subsubsubsection{Declaring templates}

Despite the fact that template declarations have CamelCase names we do
not list them as user facing because they are mainly intended for
programmers defining design solutions. Typically used either in the
\LaTeX{} kernel or in class or package files.

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewTemplateType
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewTemplateType} \Arg{type} \Arg{\# of arguments}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares a new template \meta{type}; every template and instance of
  this type takes \meta{\# of arguments} arguments when used.
  A template type can only be declared once!
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\publicreaders{diffcoeff, hustthesis, ltx-talk, sjtuthesis, sysuthesis,
  talkthemespectrum, xfrac}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareTemplateInterface
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareTemplateInterface} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{\# of arguments} \Arg{key spec}
  \end{syntax}
  Declare the interface for a template named \meta{name} of type
  \meta{type}. The \meta{\# of arguments} must match the number
  declared for \meta{type}.
%
  The \meta{key spec} specifies all keys understood by the template,
  their key-type and if applicable, a default value for each, in the
  form \meta{key}\texttt{\,:\,}\meta{key type}\texttt{\,=\,}\meta{default}.

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}
\publicreaders{acro2, diffcoeff, diffcoeff4, easybase, enotez,
  exsheets\_headings.def, fduthesis, fduthesis-en, hustthesis, ltx-talk,
  moloch-talk, njuthesis, nwafupaper, nwafuthesis, sjtuthesis,
  substances, sysuthesis, talkthemespectrum, talkthemetcolorbox,
  tamu-talk-header, tamu-talk-titlepage, tasks, xfrac}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \KeyValue
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \meta{key2} : \meta{key type} = \cs{KeyValue} \Arg{key1}
  \end{syntax}
  Refers to the value of another key of the same template. Can be
  used as default values for keys, so that one key follows another
  unless set explicitly. Can also be used in \cs{DeclareInstance} or
  \cs{EditInstance} to specify key values there.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \EditTemplateDefaults
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{EditTemplateDefaults} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{new defaults}
  \end{syntax}
  Replaces the defaults of template \meta{name} by the key--value list
  \meta{new defaults}. This affects instances declared afterwards;
  existing instances are unchanged.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}
\publicreaders{diffcoeff, diffcoeff4, talkthemetcolorbox, xfrac,
  xtemplate}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareTemplateInterfaceEquivalents
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareTemplateInterfaceEquivalents} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \oarg{date} \Arg{key spec}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares additional keys for template \meta{name} that act as
  equivalents of its base keys, e.g., as an alias or as a key that sets
  several base keys. If \meta{date} is given, the keys are
  deprecated from that date and their use produces a warning. Useful
  for renaming keys without breaking existing instances.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\publicreaders{}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareTemplateCode
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareTemplateCode} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{\# of arguments} \Arg{key bindings} \Arg{code}
  \end{syntax}
  Implements template \meta{name}: \meta{key bindings} maps each key
  of the interface to a variable (e.g.,
  \texttt{indent = \textbackslash l\_mytemplate\_indent\_dim}), and
  \meta{code} is executed when the template is used, with the
  arguments of the type as \texttt{\#1}, \ldots. Key values are
  assigned to the variables before \meta{code} (or at
  \cs{AssignTemplateKeys}).

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}
\publicreaders{acro2, diffcoeff, diffcoeff4, easybase, enotez,
  exsheets\_headings.def, fduthesis, fduthesis-en, hustthesis, ltx-talk,
  lwarp-enotez, moloch-talk, njuthesis, nwafupaper, nwafuthesis,
  sjtuthesis, substances, sysuthesis, talkthemespectrum,
  talkthemetcolorbox, tamu-talk-header, tamu-talk-titlepage, tasks,
  xfrac}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \AssignTemplateKeys
  }
  Used directly (not nested in a macro) inside the \meta{code} of
  \cs{DeclareTemplateCode} to delay the assignment of the key values
  to their variables until this point; otherwise they are assigned
  before \meta{code} starts.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}
\publicreaders{acro2, diffcoeff, diffcoeff4, easybase, enotez,
  exsheets\_headings.def, fduthesis, fduthesis-en, hustthesis,
  lwarp-enotez, njuthesis, nwafupaper, nwafuthesis, sjtuthesis,
  substances, sysuthesis, tasks}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \SetTemplateKeys,
    \SetKnownTemplateKeys
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{SetTemplateKeys} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{key settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Used inside the \meta{code} of \cs{DeclareTemplateCode} to
  override key values, typically with a key--value list passed by
  the user as an argument. \cs{SetTemplateKeys} gives an error for
  unknown keys, \cs{SetKnownTemplateKeys} stores them in
  \cs{UnusedTemplateKeys}. If used together with
  \cs{AssignTemplateKeys} the latter should come first.
\end{function}
\modifiers[SetTemplateKeys]{xtemplate-2023-10-10}
\modifiers[SetKnownTemplateKeys]{}
\publicreaders[SetTemplateKeys]{ltx-talk}
\publicreaders[SetKnownTemplateKeys]{}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \SetCurrentKnownTemplateKeys
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{SetCurrentKnownTemplateKeys} \Arg{key settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{SetKnownTemplateKeys} but uses the type and name of the
  template currently being executed. It should be used before any
  other template is called.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\publicreaders{}


\begin{variable}[readonly]
  {
    \UnusedTemplateKeys
  }
  Holds the key--value pairs that the last
  \cs{SetKnownTemplateKeys} or \cs{SetCurrentKnownTemplateKeys} did
  not know, so that they can be passed on to another template.
\end{variable}
\modifiers{}
\publicreaders{}




\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareTemplateCopy
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareTemplateCopy} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{from-name}
  \end{syntax}
  Copies the template definition with the name \meta{from-name} to the
  template with name \meta{name}.
%
  Afterwards one can alter defaults or the code implementation. In
  contrast to \cs{DeclareInstanceCopy} only limited usefulness.

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\publicreaders{diffcoeff, xfrac, xtemplate}



%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsubsection{Declaring template instances}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareInstance
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareInstance} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{template} \Arg{key settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares instance \meta{name} of \meta{type} using \meta{template},
  with the template's defaults modified by \meta{key settings}.

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \EditInstance
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{EditInstance} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{key settings}
  \end{syntax}
  Edits some or all of the key settings for the existing instance
  \meta{name} of type \meta{type}.

  Does not change the used template. If that is necessary then
  \cs{DeclareInstance} has to be used to overwrite the existing
  declaration.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}




\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareInstanceCopy
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareInstanceCopy} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{from-name}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares instance \meta{name} of \meta{type} to be a copy of the
  existing instance \meta{from-name} (of the same type).

  The declaration overwrites an existing declaration with the same
  \meta{name} without warning.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}





%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsubsection{Using instances}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \UseInstance
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{UseInstance} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \meta{arguments for type}
  \end{syntax}
  Executes instance \meta{name} of \meta{type} with as many
  \meta{arguments} as declared for the type. Gives an error if the
  instance doesn't exist.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \UseTemplate
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{UseTemplate} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{key settings}  \meta{arguments for type}
  \end{syntax}
  Uses template \meta{name} directly with the given \meta{key
  settings}, i.e., like declaring an anonymous instance and using it
  immediately. Useful if a template is needed only once.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}



\begin{function}[TF,user]
  {
    \IfInstanceExists
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{IfInstanceExistsTF} \Arg{type} \Arg{name} \Arg{true} \Arg{false}
  \end{syntax}
  Tests whether instance \meta{name} of \meta{type} has been declared.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}




%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsubsection{Showing template and instance information}



\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ShowTemplateInterface,
    \ShowTemplateDefaults,
    \ShowTemplateVariables,
    \ShowTemplateCode
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ShowTemplateInterface} \Arg{type}  \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  For the template \meta{name} of type \meta{type} the commands show the
  \begin{description}
  \item[interface] i.e., keys and associated key types
  \item[defaults] i.e., default values for the keys (if any)
  \item[variables] i.e., key bindings to variables used in code
  \item[code] i.e., the code that implements the template functionality
  \end{description}

  The display is implemented with an \cs{errmessage} so \TeX{} stops
  its processing to allow inspection.
\end{function}
\modifiers[ShowTemplateInterface]{xtemplate-2023-10-10}
\modifiers[ShowTemplateDefaults]{xtemplate-2023-10-10}
\modifiers[ShowTemplateVariables]{xtemplate-2023-10-10}
\modifiers[ShowTemplateCode]{xtemplate-2023-10-10}




\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \ShowInstanceValues
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{ShowInstanceValues} \Arg{type} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  For the instance \meta{name} of type \meta{type} all keys and their
  current values are displayed. The template that was used for the
  instance is given as a pseudo key called \verb*=from template=.


  The display is implemented with an \cs{errmessage} so \TeX{} stops
  its processing to allow inspection.
\end{function}
\modifiers{xtemplate-2023-10-10}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DebugTemplatesOn,
    \DebugTemplatesOff
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DebugTemplatesOn} ... \cs{DebugTemplatesOff}
  \end{syntax}
  Turn on (or off) debugging information about the use of templates
  and instances, i.e., messages at the point where they are used
  (which are normally suppressed for performance reasons).
\end{function}
\modifiers[DebugTemplatesOn]{}
\modifiers[DebugTemplatesOff]{}

\subsection{Low-level \TeX{} registers and streams}

The allocation commands below allocate registers globally. Use
\cs{newcounter} and \cs{newlength} for document-level counters and
lengths.

%-----------------------------------------------
\subsubsection{\TeX{} registers}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newcount,
    \newdimen,
    \newskip,
    \newmuskip,
    \newtoks
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newcount} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  A new integer (count), dimen, skip, muskip, or toks register is
  allocated and the command \meta{cmd} refers to it. No check is made
  whether \meta{cmd} is already defined (unlike \cs{newlength}). All
  registers available in the engine (normally 32768 or more) can be
  allocated.
\end{function}
\modifiers[newcount]{bussproofs, etex}
\modifiers[newdimen]{bussproofs, etex}
\modifiers[newskip]{bussproofs, etex}
\modifiers[newmuskip]{etex}
\modifiers[newtoks]{etex}

\subsubsection{Handling \TeX{}-level register allocations}

\begin{variable}[int,readonly]
  {
    \insc@unt,
    \allocationnumber
  }
  Internal counters to manage \TeX{} registers: the last insert
  number allocated (inserts are allocated downwards) and the number of
  the most recently allocated register.
\end{variable}
\modifiers[insc@unt]{}
\modifiers[allocationnumber]{}
\readers[insc@unt]{bussproofs, bytefield, etex, nath, pinlabel, seminar,
  tvz-code}
\readers[allocationnumber]{bytefield, elocalloc, etex, fspdefault.tex,
  fspolddefault.tex, inputnormalization, latexbangla-engine-luatex.tex,
  luacolor, morewrites, oz, program, regstats, shadethm}

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \alloc@
  }
  The plain \TeX{} interface for allocating registers, now implemented
  with \cs{e@alloc}. Use the \cs{new...} commands instead.
\end{function}
\modifiers{etex}
\readers{bussproofs, minitoc, pinlabel, seminar, tvz-code,
  unicode-persianmath}

\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \e@alloc
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{e@alloc} \meta{type} \meta{definer} \meta{counter} \meta{reserved} \meta{max} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Generic register allocator: increments \meta{counter}, checks it
  against \meta{max} with \cs{e@ch@ck}, and defines \meta{cmd} with
  \meta{definer} (e.g., \cs{countdef}) as the next register of
  \meta{type}. Used by all \cs{new...} register commands.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\readers{bigfoot, bytefield, elocalloc, gloss-czech.ldf,
  gloss-polish.ldf, gloss-slovak.ldf, mathfam256, mathtools, morefloats,
  msu-thesis, songs}

\begin{constant}[int]
  {
    \e@alloc@top
  }
  The highest register number available in the current engine
  (e.g., 32767 or 65535).
\end{constant}
\modifiers{}
\readers{elocalloc}



\begin{function}[int]
  {
    \e@ch@ck
  }
  Helper for \cs{e@alloc} that checks if the register limit is
  reached, skipping register numbers reserved for inserts and
  giving an error if no register is left.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}
\readers{bytefield, elocalloc}



\begin{constant}[int]
  {
    \e@insert@top
  }
  The highest register number that can be used for an insertion class
  (255 in engines with a limited number of inserts).
\end{constant}
\modifiers{}
\readers{}



\subsubsection{Manipulating \TeX{}-level registers}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \advance,
    \divide
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{advance} \meta{register} \texttt{by} \meta{value}
  \end{syntax}

  \TeX{} primitives that change the register value by adding or
  dividing (integer division, truncating). The \texttt{by} is
  optional. The change is local unless prefixed by \cs{global}. There
  is also \cs{multiply}. For more complex calculations \cs{numexpr}
  or \cs{dimexpr} are usually easier.

\end{function}

\subsubsection{\TeX{} input and output streams}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newread,
    \newwrite
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newwrite} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}

  A new read or write stream is allocated and the command \meta{cmd}
  refers to it. There are only 16 streams of each kind (in some
  engines more read streams), so they are a limited resource.

\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \openin,
    \openout
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{openin} \meta{stream} \texttt{=} \meta{file}
    \cs{immediate}\cs{openout} \meta{stream} \texttt{=} \meta{file}
  \end{syntax}
  \TeX{} primitives that open \meta{file} for reading or writing on
  \meta{stream}. Without \cs{immediate}, \cs{openout} is delayed until
  the page is shipped out. Close with \cs{closein} or \cs{closeout}.
\end{function}

  {
    \read
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{read} \meta{stream} \texttt{to} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}

  unbalanced) from \meta{stream} and defines \meta{cmd} locally with
  it. Stream numbers outside 0--15 read from the terminal. See also
  \cs{readline} (e-\TeX{}).
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \wlog,
    \protected@wlog
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{wlog} \Arg{message}
  \end{syntax}
  Writes \meta{message} to the transcript file on a line by
  itself. Commands inside \meta{message} are expanded, which may
  result in errors depending on the content. \cs{protected@wlog} is
  like \cs{wlog} but sets \cs{protect} in a suitable way so that
  robust commands behave as in \cs{typeout}.
\end{function}

%===============================================

\subsection{Plain \TeX{} leftovers}

\LaTeX\,2.09 started out as a format on top of plain \TeX{} and kept a
number of plain \TeX{} commands. Some of them have been useful in
programming \LaTeXe{} macros, though the L3 programming layer provides
much better alternatives.  A few ended up in regular use in user
documents, but with a few exceptions this is not recommended!


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \centerline,
    \leftline,
    \rightline
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{centerline} \Arg{material}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  Produces a \cs{hbox} of size \cs{hsize} and typesets the
  \meta{material} inside, either centered, flush left, or flush
  right. As a simple \cs{hbox} it does not start a paragraph (as
  \cs{mbox} or \cs{makebox} do), and in a list it ignores the
  indentation.

\end{function}

  plain-xetex-bidi.def}

\modifiers[rightline]{latex-xetex-bidi.def, lwarp, plain-xetex-bidi.def}

\begin{function}[int, deprecated]
  {
    \@@line
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@@line} \Arg{material}
  \end{syntax}
  Command to implement \cs{centerline}, \cs{leftline}, and
  \cs{rightline}.  Deprecated, do not use directly.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \clap,
    \llap,
    \rlap
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{rlap} \Arg{material}
  \end{syntax}
  %
  Puts the \meta{material} into an \cs{hbox} of zero width together
  with \cs{hss} on one or both sides. As a result, the material sticks
  out of the box without taking up any size in \LaTeX{}'s eyes. Thus
  one can overprint material or have something sticking out into the
  margin, etc. However, as this is using an \cs{hbox} no paragraph is
  started so if this command is used just in front of a paragraph it
  will appear on a line before the paragraph---not where most people
  would expect it.

  The safer \LaTeX{} equivalent would be
  \cs{makebox}\oarg{position}\texttt{\{0pt\}}\Arg{material} as this would
  always start a paragraph, if necessary.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \catcode
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{catcode} `\meta{char} \texttt{=} \meta{number}
  \end{syntax}
  \TeX{} primitive to set (or read) the category code of a character,
  i.e., how \TeX{} interprets it when reading input. The change is
  local and only affects characters read afterwards, not those already
  tokenized, e.g., in an argument.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \chardef
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{chardef} \meta{cmd} \texttt{=} \meta{number}
  \end{syntax}
  \TeX{} primitive that defines \meta{cmd} to typeset character
  \meta{number}. Since \meta{cmd} can also be used where \TeX{}
  expects a number, it is often used to define integer constants
  (0--255, or larger in Unicode engines), e.g., \cs{@xxxii}.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \dospecials
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{def}\cs{do}\#1\{\ldots\}    \cs{dospecials}
  \end{syntax}
  \cs{dospecials} calls \cs{do} for a list of typical \LaTeX{} syntax
  characters so that with an appropriate definition of \cs{do}
  something can be done for each of them, typically
  \cs{let}\cs{do}\cs{@makeother} to set up verbatim reading. The list is:

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \DeclareRelease,
    \DeclareCurrentRelease
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareRelease} \Arg{name} \Arg{date} \Arg{file}
    \cs{DeclareCurrentRelease} \Arg{name} \Arg{date}
  \end{syntax}
  Used at the top of a package or class to support rollback: each
  \cs{DeclareRelease} names an older release (\meta{name} may be
  empty), the date from which it applies, and the \meta{file}
  containing it (by convention
  \meta{package}\texttt{-}\meta{date}\texttt{.sty}).
  \cs{DeclareCurrentRelease} declares the current release and must come
  last. If a rollback date or name is requested (via the optional
  date argument of \cs{usepackage} or via \pkg{latexrelease}), the
  matching file is loaded instead.
\end{function}
\modifiers[DeclareRelease]{}
\modifiers[DeclareCurrentRelease]{}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \EndIncludeInRelease
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{IncludeInRelease}\Arg{date}\meta{cmd}\Arg{description}
    \ \ \meta{code}
    \cs{EndIncludeInRelease}
  \end{syntax}
  Ends a code block started with \cs{IncludeInRelease}. Such blocks
  are used in the kernel (and in packages) for rollback support: when
  an older format date is requested only the blocks whose \meta{date} is
  not later than the requested date are executed. For each \meta{cmd}
  the blocks are given newest first and the last one has date
  \texttt{0000/00/00}.
\end{function}
\modifiers{contract}
\publicreaders{fontaxes, scrbase, scrbase-20260202}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewModuleRelease,
    \EndModuleRelease
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewModuleRelease}\Arg{date}\Arg{name}\Arg{description}
    \ \ \meta{code}
    \cs{IncludeInRelease}\texttt{\{0000/00/00\}}\Arg{name}\Arg{description}
    \ \ \meta{undo code}
    \cs{EndModuleRelease}
  \end{syntax}
  Marks a whole new module of code (e.g., a new kernel file). When
  rolling back to a date before \meta{date} the module is skipped and
  only the \meta{undo code} is executed (which, e.g., undefines
  commands of the module).
\end{function}
\modifiers[NewModuleRelease]{}
\modifiers[EndModuleRelease]{}
\publicreaders[NewModuleRelease]{}
\publicreaders[EndModuleRelease]{}

  must use the public hooks instead.
\end{constant}

  {

  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{IfFileExists} \Arg{file} \Arg{true} \Arg{false}
  \end{syntax}

  directory, the \cs{input@path}, or the \TeX{} search path) and
  executes \meta{true} or \meta{false}. In \meta{true} the found file
  name is available as \cs{@filef@und}. See also \cs{InputIfFileExists}.
\end{function}

  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@ifnextchar} \meta{char} \Arg{true} \Arg{false}

  Looks at the next non-space token in the input: if it is

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@dblarg
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@dblarg} \meta{cmd}
  \end{syntax}
  Calls \meta{cmd}, which must take an optional and a mandatory
  argument, such that if the optional argument is missing, the
  mandatory argument is used for it too. E.g., \cs{section} uses it
  so that the heading text is also the default for the table of
  contents entry.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@testopt
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@testopt} \meta{cmd} \Arg{default}
  \end{syntax}
  If the next token is \texttt{[}, calls \meta{cmd}; otherwise calls
  \meta{cmd}\texttt{[}\meta{default}\texttt{]}. Implements commands
  whose first argument is optional, e.g.,
  \cs{def}\cs[no-index]{foo}\texttt{\{}\cs{@testopt}\cs[no-index]{@foo}\texttt{\{default\}\}}.
\end{function}

  }

  \end{syntax}

  with strength \meta{number} from \texttt{0} (slight) to \texttt{4}
  (forced, or prohibited); default is \texttt{4}. In a paragraph, the
  break applies after the current line.

  penalties to 10000 (within the current group). Breaks between
  paragraphs remain possible; it is rarely effective, so
  \cs{nopagebreak} or a \texttt{minipage} is often a better choice.

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@bsphack,
    \@esphack
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@bsphack} \meta{material} \cs{@esphack}
  \end{syntax}

  \cs{label}, \cs{index}, \cs{marginpar}) so that they don't add extra
  space: if there was a space before \cs{@bsphack}, the space after
  \cs{@esphack} is ignored. Only active in horizontal mode.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \addvspace
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{addvspace} \Arg{skip}
  \end{syntax}
  Adds vertical space of \meta{skip}, but if the preceding item was
  also space added by \cs{addvspace}, only the larger of the two is
  used (so that, e.g., consecutive lists or headings don't accumulate
  space). Must be used in vertical mode; in a paragraph it ends the
  paragraph first, but in an \cs{hbox} it gives an error. Used by
  lists and sectioning commands.
\end{function}
\modifiers{adfathesis, bxcalcize, classicthesis, lhelp, ndsu-thesis,
  ndsu-thesis-2022, rhode-island-thesis, tocbasic, toptesi, tvz-hax,
  unbtex}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \addpenalty
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{addpenalty} \Arg{penalty}
  \end{syntax}
  Adds a \meta{penalty} in vertical mode in front of the preceding
  space (added by \cs{addvspace}), so that a page break at that point
  removes the space. Does nothing if \cs{if@nobreak} is true or in a
  minipage. Used, e.g., before headings.
\end{function}
\modifiers{tocbasic}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \vspace,
    \hspace
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{vspace} * \Arg{skip}
    \cs{hspace} * \Arg{skip}
  \end{syntax}
  Add vertical or horizontal space of \meta{skip}, which may contain
  stretch and shrink (and \pkg{calc} expressions). Space added at a
  page or line break is normally discarded; the star forms keep it.
  \cs{vspace} in a paragraph adds the space after the current line.
\end{function}

  eqnlines, extletter, facsimile, letteracdp, lettre, ltxgrid,
  revtex4-1, revtex4-2, scrletter, scrlttr2, sysuthesis}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \nobreakdashes
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{nobreakdashes}\texttt{--}
  \end{syntax}
  Placed directly before a hyphen or dash, prevents a line break after
  it (e.g., in \texttt{1}\cs{nobreakdashes}\texttt{--3}), while still
  allowing hyphenation of the following word. Use it only in front of
  \texttt{-}, \texttt{--}, or \texttt{---}.
\end{function}
\modifiers{}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \nobreakspace
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{nobreakspace}
  \end{syntax}
  A non-breaking space, i.e., the command behind \texttt{\textasciitilde}.
  Also used for the Unicode character U+00A0.
\end{function}

  ltugboat, ltugcomn, pittetd, proofgraph, skrapport, zugferd}


\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \@
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \texttt{CD}\cs{@}\texttt{. etc.}\cs{@}
  \end{syntax}
  Adjusts the space factor: before a period it marks the period as
  ending a sentence (e.g., after an uppercase letter), after a period
  it marks it as not ending a sentence. Only relevant when
  \cs{nonfrenchspacing} is in effect.
\end{function}

\subsection{From File: ltcounts.dtx}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \newcounteralias
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{newcounteralias} \Arg{alias} \Arg{counter}
  \end{syntax}
  Declares \meta{alias} as an alias of the existing \meta{counter}:
  both share the same value, and the representations of \meta{alias}
  (\cs{the\meta{alias}} etc.) use those of \meta{counter}. Useful,
  e.g., for theorem-like environments numbered in one sequence
  but referenced with different names.
\end{function}
\modifiers{aliascnt}
\publicreaders{keytheorems, pseudo}




\begin{function}[]
  {
    \@stpelt
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{@stpelt} \Arg{counter}
  \end{syntax}
  Resets \meta{counter} (to $-1$ and then steps it, so that counters
  reset within it are reset as well). Used as \cs{@elt} when
  \cs{stepcounter} processes the reset list.
\end{function}
\modifiers{biditools, caption3\_2010-01-14, caption3\_2011-11-01,

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \DeclareFontSeriesChangeRule,
    \DeclareFontShapeChangeRule
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{DeclareFontSeriesChangeRule} \Arg{current} \Arg{request} \Arg{result} \Arg{alternative}
  \end{syntax}
  Define how \cs{fontseries} (or \cs{fontshape}) combines the
  \meta{current} value with a \meta{request}, e.g., that requesting
  \texttt{b} while the current series is \texttt{c} (condensed) gives
  \texttt{bc}. If \meta{result} doesn't exist in the font family,
  \meta{alternative} is tried; if neither exists or there is no rule,
  \meta{request} is used. Mainly for font support packages.
\end{function}
\modifiers[DeclareFontSeriesChangeRule]{}
\modifiers[DeclareFontShapeChangeRule]{}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \itshape,
    \normalshape,
    \scshape,
    \slshape,
    \sscshape,
    \swshape,
    \ulcshape,
    \upshape
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \Arg{\cs{itshape} \meta{text}}
  \end{syntax}
  Declarations selecting the italic, normal (\cs{shapedefault}),
  small caps, slanted, spaced small caps, swash, upper/lowercase, or
  upright shape. They combine with the current shape where it makes
  sense, e.g., \cs{itshape} after \cs{scshape} gives italic small
  caps if available. Commands with argument are \cs{textit} etc.
\end{function}

  requested \meta{series} is combined with the current one according

  \end{syntax}

  \cs{fontencoding}, \cs{fontfamily}, \cs{fontseries},

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \begin,
    \end
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{begin}\Arg{name}\meta{argument(s)} ... \cs{end}\Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Start and end the environment \meta{name}. \cs{begin} opens a
  group, executes the environment hooks and \cs[no-index]{\meta{name}}
  (which picks up the arguments); \cs{end} executes
  \cs[no-index]{end\meta{name}}, checks that \meta{name} matches the
  innermost open environment (otherwise an error is given), and
  closes the group. Hence all local settings inside an environment
  are undone at its end.
\end{function}

\begin{function}[user]
  {
    \document,
    \enddocument
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{begin}\Arg{document}  \meta{document body} \cs{end}\Arg{document}
  \end{syntax}
  The \texttt{document} environment. \cs{begin}\texttt{\{document\}}
  ends the preamble: it reads the \texttt{.aux} file, runs the
  \texttt{begindocument} hooks, and disables preamble-only commands.
  \cs{end}\texttt{\{document\}} outputs the remaining material, runs
  the \texttt{enddocument} hooks, writes and checks the \texttt{.aux}
  file (e.g., for changed labels), and ends the run.
\end{function}

\subsection{From File: lttagging.dtx}

The commands below are always available, so packages can use them
whether or not tagging is active; without tagging most do nothing.

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \SuspendTagging,
    \ResumeTagging
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{SuspendTagging}\Arg{label} \meta{material} \cs{ResumeTagging}\Arg{label}
  \end{syntax}
  Stop (and restart) tagging, e.g., around trial typesetting that is
  done several times or thrown away (as in measuring with
  \cs{settowidth}). The \meta{label} is only used in debugging
  messages and is not expanded.
\end{function}
\modifiers[SuspendTagging]{}
\modifiers[ResumeTagging]{}
\publicreaders[SuspendTagging]{gia-handout, microtype, pdfcomment,
  pdfpages, sillypage, tabulary, tocloft, xltabular}
\publicreaders[ResumeTagging]{gia-handout, pdfcomment, pdfpages,
  sillypage, tabulary, tocloft, xltabular}


\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewTaggingSocket,
    \NewTaggingSocketPlug,
    \AssignTaggingSocketPlug
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewTaggingSocket} \Arg{name} \Arg{number of inputs}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{NewSocket}, \cs{NewSocketPlug}, and \cs{AssignSocketPlug},
  but for sockets named \texttt{tagsupport/\meta{name}} (the prefix
  is added automatically). \cs{NewTaggingSocket} also sets up the
  default plug used when tagging is not active.
\end{function}
\modifiers[NewTaggingSocket]{}
\modifiers[NewTaggingSocketPlug]{}
\modifiers[AssignTaggingSocketPlug]{}
\publicreaders[NewTaggingSocket]{algorithmlite, hawkdraw,
  hawkdraw-nodes.code.tex, linguistix-glossing, ltx-talk, pdfcomment,
  rpgicons-l3, rpgicons-pgf, sblarticle, sblbook, sblreport, tagpdf,
  tcolorbox}
\publicreaders[NewTaggingSocketPlug]{algorithmlite, hawkdraw,
  hawkdraw-nodes.code.tex, linguistix-glossing, ltx-talk, pdfcomment,
  rpgicons-l3, rpgicons-pgf, sblarticle, sblbook, sblreport, tagpdf,
  tagpdfdocu-patches, tcolorbox}
\publicreaders[AssignTaggingSocketPlug]{algorithmlite,
  gradbars-tblr-tagging, hawkdraw, hawkdraw-nodes.code.tex,
  linguistix-glossing, ltx-talk, pdfcomment, rpgicons-l3, rpgicons-pgf,
  sblarticle, sblbook, sblreport, tagpdf, tagpdfdocu-patches, tcolorbox}



\begin{function}[]
  {
    \UseTaggingSocket,
    \UseExpandableTaggingSocket
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{UseTaggingSocket} \Arg{name} \meta{inputs}
  \end{syntax}
  Like \cs{UseSocket} for \texttt{tagsupport/\meta{name}}, but if
  tagging is suspended or not active the socket is bypassed: with no
  input nothing happens, with one input the input is returned
  unchanged. The expandable variant can be used in expansion contexts
  (with plugs that are expandable).
\end{function}
\modifiers[UseTaggingSocket]{mitthesis, tagpdf, unhook.tex}
\modifiers[UseExpandableTaggingSocket]{tagpdf}
\publicreaders[UseTaggingSocket]{algorithmlite, array-xetex-bidi.def,

\begin{function}[]
  {
    \NewStructureName,
    \UseStructureName
  }
  \begin{syntax}
    \cs{NewStructureName} \Arg{name}
    \cs{UseStructureName} \Arg{name}
  \end{syntax}
  Declare a symbolic structure name (with initial value
  \texttt{NonStruct}) and expand to the tag stored for it. This allows
  documents to change the tag used for a structure (e.g.,
  \texttt{Chapter} instead of \texttt{Sect}) with
  \cs{AssignStructureRole}.
\end{function}
\modifiers[NewStructureName]{}
\modifiers[UseStructureName]{}
